articles.title: The Future Supreme Court Justice Had Some Pithy Advice For The President
articles.content:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day!

In July 1864, Confederate forces raided the edge of Washington, and President Abraham Lincoln rode out to a fort to watch and stood up on the parapet, stovepipe hat and all, in plain view of Confederate sharpshooters. It remains the only time a sitting U.S. president came under direct enemy fire. As the story goes, a young Union officer — a 23-year-old Oliver Wendell Holmes, then an aide-de-camp, gave what advice to Lincoln?

Hint: Though the tale is very likely apocryphal, and many people claimed to give Lincoln similar advice, the story has entered American folklore.

See the answer on the next page.

articles.title: Stat(s) Of The Week: Stress Takes A Toll
articles.content:
Seventy percent of lawyers have left jobs because of adverse effects on their mental or physical well-being, according to a new study.
The Illinois Lawyers Assistance Program surveyed more than 6,700 lawyers and judges across the state about mental health, workplace stress, substance abuse, and gambling issues.
Nearly two-thirds of lawyers surveyed (66%) believe their workplace has a negative impact on their mental, health, physical health, or overall wellness and would consider leaving their job. And 70% said they previously left a job because of its impact on their well-being, with 82% citing too much stress.
According to the study, age is “a major factor” related to work stress experiences, with 31% of attorneys between 25 and 35 years old reporting that their workplace had a negative impact on their well-being, compared, for example, to 24% of lawyers aged 36 to 45 and 18% of lawyers aged 56 to 65.
Younger lawyers also more frequently reported mental health concerns. Overall, one in five lawyers surveyed rated their mental health as fair or poor. Among lawyers aged 25 to 35, the ratio jumps to one in three.
The Weight of Practice | Illinois Lawyers’ Mental Health Study [Illinois Lawyers’ Assistance Program]

articles.title: Small Time Entries Can Add Up To Substantial Revenues For Law Firms
articles.content:
I recently had occasion to review another lawyer’s invoices in connection with a case I was handling. As I examined the bills, I noticed that the attorney had recorded dozens of 0.1-hour time entries for relatively minor tasks performed during the representation. These entries included activities that many attorneys might not even think to record, such as reviewing short emails, sending brief correspondence, and addressing small issues that arose during the course of the matter. Although each entry represented only six minutes or less of work, the cumulative value of these entries was substantial. The experience reminded me that lawyers can leave a surprising amount of money on the table when they fail to record smaller increments of billable time.
Most attorneys understand the importance of recording the hours they spend drafting motions, conducting depositions, appearing in court, and performing other substantial tasks. However, lawyers also spend considerable time each day performing smaller tasks that are necessary to advance their clients’ interests. Attorneys might answer a quick question from a client, review a short email from opposing counsel, or consider how a new development affects litigation strategy. Since these activities often take only a few minutes, lawyers may not think they are worth recording. Nevertheless, these smaller tasks are legitimate legal work when they are reasonably necessary to a representation, and attorneys should not automatically disregard this time.
The financial impact of recording smaller time entries can be significant. For instance, an attorney who bills $400 an hour generates $40 in revenue for each 0.1-hour entry. If that attorney records just five additional legitimate 0.1-hour entries each workday, this amounts to $200 in additional daily billings. Over the course of 250 working days, these entries would represent $50,000 in additional annual billings, assuming the time is ultimately collected. For a law firm with ten attorneys who each record similar amounts of previously overlooked time, the potential additional annual billings could reach $500,000.
Of course, lawyers should never manufacture billable time or record more time than they actually spend performing work. Billing practices must comply with ethical obligations, client agreements, and applicable billing guidelines. If an attorney spends two minutes on a task, that does not necessarily justify billing six minutes, particularly if the client requires actual-time billing or prohibits minimum increments. Similarly, lawyers should not divide related activities into multiple entries merely to inflate the amount of time billed. The goal should always be to accurately record legitimate work rather than to increase invoices through questionable billing practices.
One reason smaller billing entries may go unrecorded is that attorneys often do not appreciate how much time they spend on minor tasks throughout the day. A lawyer might read an email while walking between meetings, answer a client’s question over the telephone, or review a document for a few minutes before turning to another matter. By the end of the day, the attorney may have forgotten these activities entirely. Even when lawyers remember performing these tasks, they might decide that recording the time is not worth the effort. However, when this happens repeatedly, the financial consequences can become significant.
Law firms can address this problem by encouraging attorneys to record their time contemporaneously rather than attempting to reconstruct their activities at the end of the day or week. Modern billing software makes it relatively easy to enter time immediately after completing a task, and attorneys should develop habits that allow them to capture legitimate billable work without interrupting their workflow. Firms can also educate lawyers about the cumulative financial impact of small billing entries so that attorneys understand why accurate timekeeping matters. This is particularly important for smaller law firms, where relatively modest increases in collected revenue can have a meaningful impact on profitability.
There is also a psychological component to this issue. Attorneys sometimes feel uncomfortable charging clients for tasks that take only a few minutes, especially when they have developed close relationships with those clients. I certainly understand this instinct, and there are situations in which writing off time makes good business sense. However, lawyers should distinguish between accurately recording time and deciding whether to charge a client for that work. Recording legitimate time gives attorneys and law firms the information they need to make informed billing decisions, while failing to record the time at all eliminates that option.
Naturally, not every small task should result in a separate charge. Some client billing guidelines prohibit certain entries, and lawyers should exercise professional judgment about what work is reasonable to bill. Moreover, attorneys should be mindful that excessive or poorly described small entries can frustrate clients and create disputes over invoices. Transparency and reasonableness should remain central to every firm’s billing practices.
Ultimately, the invoices I recently reviewed demonstrated how much financial value can be associated with relatively small amounts of legal work. A single 0.1-hour entry might not seem particularly important, but dozens of such entries over the course of a representation can add up to substantial sums. Lawyers should not be so focused on recording large blocks of billable time that they overlook the smaller tasks that occupy much of their workdays. When accurately recorded, reasonably billed, and ultimately collected, these small entries can make a big difference to a law firm’s bottom line.
Jordan Rothman is a partner of The Rothman Law Firm, a full-service New York and New Jersey law firm. He is also the founder of Student Debt Diaries, a website discussing how he paid off his student loans. You can reach Jordan through email at jordan@rothman.law.

articles.title: AI Won’t Make Lawyering Faster. It Will Make It Different.
articles.content:
Everyone expects AI to make legal work faster. Clients expect it most of all, and some now expect lower bills to follow. Joe Patrice of Above the Law observes that clients want faster and cheaper results regardless of what AI realistically delivers. We need to manage those expectations now, before they harden into budgets.
In my experience, AI does not always get the work done faster. It gets the work done differently. The early evidence points the same way. In “Alex Su Named President Of Latitude As Flex Legal Staffing Market Booms,” Patrice notes that so far AI seems to be increasing the time lawyers work. Part of that may be lawyers frantically editing to avoid the next AI hallucination headline. Part may be that AI uncovers new counterarguments and research rabbit holes that someone has to chase down. Either way, the time does not disappear. It moves.
Su describes where it moves in Latitude’s announcement of his promotion. “As routine work gets automated, the work that’s left for legal teams to handle is more complex, higher stakes, and less predictable, and clients need to be able to bring in support quickly when it hits.” Patrice adds that a competent first draft may no longer be scarce, while the skill to edit it into something presentable will be. Latitude’s growth suggests legal teams are covering bursts of complex work with flexible talent because no one is sure what staffing should look like in an AI world.
Pricing is unsettled too. In a recent Everlaw interview, “What Comes After the Billable Hour? Ken Callander Says Firms Should Charge for Value, Not Time,” Petra Pasternak spoke with Ken Callander of Value Strategies. Callander argued that AI is pushing legal work toward value-based pricing. He helped move much of Uber’s legal work off hourly billing. As Today’s general counsel summarized, he expects contracts, immigration, employment, and real estate work to shift toward AI and other alternatives to traditional firms. In his view, highly specialized matters will keep time-based pricing.
I am less certain the billable hour is going away. It has survived many predicted deaths. Whatever the pricing model, a harder question sits beneath it. If AI changes what legal work looks like, it changes who does the work and how they learn to do it. As a GC who has also taught law students, I think that question deserves more attention than it gets.
The Speed Misconception
AI can help produce drafts in seconds. It is after that when the real work begins. Someone has to check the citations and confirm the cases say what the draft claims. Someone has to test the reasoning against the facts and spot what the tool missed or invented. The validation is where the lawyer earns the fee. The quality of the final product improves, and so does the time it takes to get there right.
Whether a firm bills by the hour or by the deliverable, the value lies in the judgment applied to the draft. A draft generated in seconds is worth little until a lawyer has tested it. Firms that want to keep client trust need to do two things. First, quantify the value they deliver in terms clients recognize, such as exposure reduced, deals closed, and risk avoided. Second, show clients how they validate AI-assisted work. I want to know how a firm guards against complacency, protects privilege, and guards against over-reliance on the tool. A firm that can’t answer that question is selling me speed, and speed alone is, quite frankly, dangerous.
The Replacement Misconception
AI won’t replace lawyers. It will change how we do the work and how we train new lawyers. The second change matters more.
Patrice notes that the entry-level work junior lawyers historically performed is getting pushed to the bots, and Biglaw associate classes are getting smaller. That should worry anyone who cares about where the next generation of lawyers comes from.
I remember being a paralegal and then a junior associate. I scoured documents and case law and prepared memos and chronologies. I remember how heavily that responsibility weighed on me. I had the technical skills. I did not yet have the legal judgment. I was afraid a partner would rely on my work and I would get something wrong.
Through repetition, under supervision, I learned what mattered and what didn’t. I learned what a partner would ask before the partner asked it.
If junior lawyers no longer build judgment by grinding through document review and research memos, where will they build it?
Recalibrating The Senior-Junior Relationship
I believe new lawyers will learn by digging into how AI does the work and validating it. The junior lawyer’s job shifts from producing the first draft to questioning it. Why did the tool reach this conclusion? What authority supports it? What did it leave out? Would this hold up in front of a judge, a regulator, or opposing counsel? That is a harder skill to teach than drafting a memo from scratch. It also requires senior lawyers to change. Partners and GCs can no longer simply review the junior lawyer’s output. They need to review the junior lawyer’s validation process. They need to explain why they trust one answer and push back on another.
The senior-junior relationship was always an apprenticeship. In the AI era, it has to become an apprenticeship in judgment.
A Word To Professors
Law schools need to rethink this too. Professors should allow students to use AI, provided the professor will actually examine the work and require the student to validate it.
If we allow AI without demanding validation, we teach students bad habits. They learn to trust output they don’t understand. Those habits are hard to break, even for students who manage to pass the bar. Their future employers and clients will pay for that.
Banning AI isn’t the answer either. Our students will use these tools on their first day of practice. Our job is to make sure they use them as lawyers.
We Have Been Here Before
I am old enough to remember the birth of the internet and the move from books to online research. People worried then that lawyers would lose the ability to research. Instead, the profession adapted. The best lawyers learned to use the new tools without giving up the judgment the tools couldn’t supply.
AI is a tool like any other tool. It is more capable than anything we have had before, so the stakes are higher. Lawyers who treat it as a shortcut will get caught. Lawyers who treat it as a starting point and validate the work will deliver better results than ever.
The work may not get faster. It will get better, and clients will pay for that.
Lisa Lang is an accomplished in-house lawyer and thought leader dedicated to empowering fellow legal professionals. She offers insights and resources tailored for in-house counsel through her website and blog, Why This, Not That™ (www.lawyerlisalang.com). Lisa actively engages with the legal community via LinkedIn, sharing her expertise and fostering meaningful connections.
